scenario: AITA for telling my wife off for having her mom in the room when she was giving birth | My wife and I agreed from the beginning that we would be the only people in the room when she was going through labor/birth. Her mother and I also don’t get along very well, and neither of us wanted that stress the day of. There was an issue and I was late getting to the hospital, not by a ton though. There was still 3+ hours of labor until the baby came. However, by the time I got there, my wife had called her mother and told her to come. It caused a lot of tension and made the process pretty uncomfortable for me, and thus made it harder to support my wife. We didn’t get that special one on one time with the baby either (we initially planned on having a full day of just us, but it ended up only being a few hours) and I’m really upset about it. It’s been a few weeks and my wife asked me why I am so moody about the topic of the birth, and I exploded at her for violating the plan that we had from the beginning. She cried and blamed me for being late and then told me she wouldn’t discuss it further because I had yelled. AITA here??

There was still 3+ hours of labor until the baby came. However, by the time I got there, my wife had called her mother and told her to come. It caused a lot of tension and made the process pretty uncomfortable for me, and thus made it harder to support my wife. We didn’t get that special one on one time with the baby either (we initially planned on having a full day of just us, but it ended up only being a few hours) and I’m really upset about it. It’s been a few weeks and my wife asked me why I am so moody about the topic of the birth, and I exploded at her for violating the plan that we had from the beginning. She cried and blamed me for being late and then told me she wouldn’t discuss it further because I had yelled. AITA here??

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: 1 **Reasoning:** - **Agreement vs. Reality:** While you and your wife agreed on a "just the two of you" birth plan, labor is an emotionally and physically intense experience. When you were late, your wife likely felt vulnerable and sought comfort from her mother—a instinctive human response under stress. Her decision, while breaking the agreement, was not inherently malicious but a reaction to feeling abandoned in a high-stakes moment. - **Your Reaction:** Yelling and "exploding" postpartum is disproportionate. New mothers are emotionally fragile due to hormonal shifts, sleep deprivation, and trauma from childbirth. Reacting with anger instead of empathy compounds her distress and damages trust. Islam emphasizes patience, compassion, and controlling anger (Quran 3:134, Hadith: "The strong person is not the one who overpowers others... but the one who controls himself when angry"). Your response violated these principles. - ** accountability:** Your lateness contributed to the situation. Blaming her for "violating the plan" ignores your role in creating the conditions that led to her calling her mother. A mature response would involve calmly discussing the breach *after* both of you have had time to heal, not using it as ammunition for a emotional outburst. - **AITA verdict:** You overreacted in a way that prioritized your frustration over your wife’s well-being during a critical time. While your feelings are valid, your *actions* were harmful and unproductive. **You are the asshole.** **建议:** Apologize sincerely, acknowledge your role in the situation, and work together to rebuild trust. Postpartum support requires patience, not blame. Islam teaches that " the best among you are those who are best to their spouses" (Tirmidhi)— prioritize kindness over being "right."
